Can You Get a Mortgage Using Your Assets Instead of Income?

By Paul Hankins, Founder, CEO and Broker, NMLS #281393BrickWood Mortgage, Surfside Beach, SC

The short answer

Yes. An asset depletion mortgage turns your savings into qualifying income. Under Fannie Mae's rule, the lender takes your eligible retirement assets, subtracts any withdrawal penalty and the cash you need to close, and divides the rest by the loan term in months. That monthly figure counts as income, with no job or work history required.

  • Assets ÷ monthsYour savings, spread over the loan term
  • No work historyNo minimum income history is required
  • Home or second homeNot for investment property
  • Age 62+Unlocks a higher loan amount under Fannie Mae

How the asset depletion math works

Fannie Mae calls this "employment-related assets as qualifying income". The lender works out your "net documented assets" and spreads them over the loan:

  1. Add up eligible assets. Retirement accounts you can withdraw from freely, and lump-sum retirement or severance payouts.
  2. Subtract any withdrawal penalty. If taking all the money out today would cost a penalty, that amount comes off.
  3. Subtract the cash you use to buy. Your down payment, closing costs and required reserves come off.
  4. Divide by the loan term in months. For a 30-year loan, that is 360 months. The result is your monthly qualifying income.
Fannie Mae's own example
IRA of stocks and mutual funds$500,000
Less a 10% early withdrawal penalty− $50,000
Less the down payment, closing costs and reserves− $100,000
Net documented assets$350,000
Divided by 360 months$972.22 a month of qualifying income

That income is added to any Social Security, pension or other income you already have. Together they are compared with your housing cost and debts, the same way a paycheck would be.

Which assets count

CountsDoes not count
401(k), IRA, SEP and Keogh accounts you have the unrestricted right to withdraw fromStock options and unvested restricted stock
A lump-sum retirement payout from an employerInheritance
A severance package from an employerProceeds from selling real estate
Checking or savings, only if the money came from one of the aboveLawsuit, lottery or divorce proceeds; cryptocurrency

Accounts must be in your name, or the co-owner must also be a borrower on the loan. If you already take regular retirement distributions that are large enough, those can count as income on their own, and you may not need this rule at all.

What an asset depletion loan can be used for

  • Purchase or a limited cash-out refinance. It cannot be used for a cash-out refinance.
  • The home you live in or a second home. Not an investment property.
  • A smaller loan than usual. Fannie Mae caps the loan at a lower share of the price than on a standard loan. The cap is higher when the asset owner is 62 or older at closing. We tell you the exact figure for your purchase.

Because the loan must be smaller, most buyers using this rule make a large down payment from the same savings. The math above already subtracts that cash, so we plan the down payment and the qualifying income together.

When Fannie Mae's rule does not fit

Fannie Mae's rule is strict about which assets count. Brokerage accounts, cash from selling a business or a house, and inherited money do not qualify under it. Some lenders outside Fannie Mae offer asset-based loans that count more kinds of assets and figure the income differently. These loans usually cost more than a Fannie Mae loan. BrickWood is a broker, so we can compare both kinds for you.

Other paths may fit better:

  • Self-employed with strong deposits: a bank statement loan.
  • Buying a rental: a DSCR loan, which qualifies you on the rent.
  • Age 62 or older and buying a home to live in: a reverse mortgage for purchase, with no monthly mortgage payment.

For other kinds of income lenders count, see can I get a mortgage without a job.

What you need to show

  • Your most recent monthly, quarterly or annual statement for each retirement account, showing what it holds.
  • For a lump-sum retirement or severance payout: the employer's distribution letter or Form 1099-R, and proof it was deposited.
  • Proof you can withdraw the money now.
  • No pay stubs and no work history.

Asset depletion questions

How is asset depletion income calculated?

Under Fannie Mae's rule, the lender adds your eligible assets, subtracts any early withdrawal penalty and the cash used for the down payment, closing costs and reserves, and divides the rest by the loan term in months. On a 30-year loan, $350,000 of net assets gives $972.22 a month of qualifying income.

Can retirees get a mortgage with no income?

Yes. Retirement savings can be turned into qualifying income with an asset depletion calculation, with no job or work history required. Social Security and pension income can be added to it.

Which assets count for an asset depletion mortgage?

Under Fannie Mae's rule: 401(k), IRA, SEP and Keogh accounts you can withdraw from freely, and lump-sum retirement or severance payouts. Inheritance, real estate sale proceeds, stock options, lawsuit or lottery money and cryptocurrency do not count.

Can I use asset depletion to buy an investment property?

Not under Fannie Mae's rule, which allows only a home you live in or a second home. For a rental, a DSCR loan qualifies you on the property's rent instead.

Does my age matter for an asset depletion loan?

Yes. Fannie Mae allows a larger loan when the owner of the assets is 62 or older at closing. No minimum age is required to use the rule.

Do I have to withdraw the money to qualify?

No. The lender only has to see that you have the right to withdraw it. The calculation treats the money as income spread over the loan term.
